comparisons.peer_summary: Citigroup's CET1 Capital ratio increased to 13.6% as of December 31, 2024, from 13.4% in 2023, driven by net income and a decrease in risk-weighted assets, partially offset by dividends, share repurchases, and AOCI movements.
comparisons.comparison: Both BAC and C report on CET1 capital movements and RWA trends under the Standardized Approach. BAC reports an absolute increase in CET1 capital ($6.2 billion) and an increase in RWA ($44.5 billion), driven by client activity and lending. In contrast, C reports an increase in its CET1 capital ratio (13.4% to 13.6%) driven by net income and a *decrease* in RWA. While both cite earnings/net income as a driver for capital strengthening, BAC's capital base grew alongside asset growth, whereas C's ratio improved partly due to risk weight reduction.

sentences.text: At December 31, 2024, CET1 capital was $201.1 billion, an increase of $6.2 billion from December 31, 2023, primarily due to earnings, partially offset by capital distributions.

RWA under the Standardized approach, which yielded the lower CET1 capital ratio at December 31, 2024, increased $44.5 billion during 2024 to $1,696 billion primarily driven by client activity in Global Markets and lending activity in GWIM, Global Banking and Consumer Banking.
Citigroup's CET1 Capital ratio was 13.6% as of December 31, 2024, compared to 13.4% as of December 31, 2023, based on the Basel III Standardized Approach for determining risk weighted assets (RWA).

The increase was primarily driven by net income and a decrease in RWA, partially offset by the payment of common and preferred dividends, as well as common share repurchases and net adverse movements in Accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI).

comparisons.peer_summary: The firm returned $11.80 billion to shareholders via repurchases and dividends in 2024, while maintaining strong regulatory capital positions with a CET1 ratio of 15.0% under Standardized Rules and 15.3% under Advanced Rules as of December 2024.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address regulatory capital ratios and capital returns in 2024. BAC provides absolute capital figures ($201.1 billion CET1) and notes that distributions offset earnings. GS highlights its CET1 ratio (15.0% under Standardized Rules) and quantifies capital returns ($11.80 billion to shareholders). BAC explains capital changes through earnings and distributions, while GS focuses on the ratio outcome and the magnitude of shareholder returns.

sentences.text: At December 31, 2024, CET1 capital was $201.1 billion, an increase of $6.2 billion from December 31, 2023, primarily due to earnings, partially offset by capital distributions.
Tier 1 capital increased $135 million primarily driven by the increase in CET1 capital, partially offset by preferred stock redemptions.
During 2024, we returned a total of $11.80 billion of capital to common shareholders, including $8.00 billion of common share repurchases and $3.80 billion of common stock dividends.
As of December 2024, our CET1 capital ratio was 15.0% under the Standardized Capital Rules and 15.3% under the Advanced Capital Rules.

BAC attributes its $44.5 billion RWA increase to client activity in Global Markets and lending in GWIM, Global Banking, and Consumer Banking. MS attributes its Credit risk RWA increase primarily to growth in Corporate lending and Securities financing transactions. Both firms show RWA expansion driven by lending and financing activities, though BAC includes specific business line details (GWIM) not present in MS's summarized drivers.

sentences.text: RWA under the Standardized approach, which yielded the lower CET1 capital ratio at December 31, 2024, increased $44.5 billion during 2024 to $1,696 billion primarily driven by client activity in Global Markets and lending activity in GWIM, Global Banking and Consumer Banking.
In 2024, Credit risk RWA increased under both the Standardized and Advanced Approaches.

Under the Standardized Approach, the increase was primarily due to higher Securities financing transactions, growth in Corporate lending, as well as an increase in Other credit risk driven by securitizations.
